items.readable_text:
Content:
Two lines are perpendicular if they intersect at a right angle. For example, the lines [MATH: {\color{red}y = 2x - 1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+5}] shown below are perpendicular:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/81aa2de5645d05769b37848e83376801]

Content:
We can tell whether two lines are perpendicular by looking at their slopes. In general,

Content:
> If two lines are perpendicular, then the product of their slopes is equal to [MATH: -1.]

Content:
We see this with the two lines graphed above: the lines [MATH: {\color{red}y = 2x - 1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+5}] have slopes [MATH: \color{red}2] and [MATH: {\color{blue}-\dfrac{1}{2}},] respectively. If we take the product of the slopes, we get

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}{\left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) }} = -1.]

Content:
Watch out! The only exception is for horizontal and vertical lines. Horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular, but the slope of a vertical line is undefined, so we cannot multiply it by anything.

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following lines is perpendicular to [MATH: y= -\dfrac{2}{5}x-3?]

  1. [MATH: y = 5x + 1]

  2. [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3]

  3. [MATH: y = -\dfrac{x}{2} + 5]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following lines is perpendicular to [MATH: y= -\dfrac{2}{5}x-3?]

1. [MATH: y = 5x + 1]
2. [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3]
3. [MATH: y = -\dfrac{x}{2} + 5]

sections.normalized_html:
For the two lines to be perpendicular, their slopes must multiply to [MATH: -1.]

The line [MATH: y=-\dfrac{2}{5}x-3] is in slope-intercept form, and its slope is [MATH: -\dfrac{2}{5}.]

Looking at the answer choices, the line [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3] has a slope of [MATH: \dfrac{5}{2}.]

Multiplying the slopes together, we have

[MATH: \left( -\dfrac{2}{5}\right) \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} = -1.]

Since the slopes multiply to [MATH: -1,] we conclude that the line [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3] is perpendicular to the given line.

So, the correct answer is "II only".

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following lines is perpendicular to [MATH: 4x - 2y = 10?]

  1. [MATH: y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3]

  2. [MATH: y = -4x + 1]

  3. [MATH: y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x -5]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following lines is perpendicular to [MATH: 4x - 2y = 10?]

1. [MATH: y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3]
2. [MATH: y = -4x + 1]
3. [MATH: y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x -5]

sections.normalized_html:
For the two lines to be perpendicular, their slopes must multiply to [MATH: -1.]

To find the slope of the given line [MATH: 4x - 2y = 10,] we convert to slope-intercept form: [MATH: 4x − 2y|= 10; − 2y|= − 4x + 10; y|= 2x − 5]

In slope-intercept form, the slope is the [MATH: x]-coefficient. So, the slope of the given line is [MATH: 2.]

Looking at the answer choices, the line [MATH: y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x -5] has a slope of [MATH: -\dfrac{1}{2}.]

Multiplying the slopes together, we have

[MATH: 2 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -1.]

Since the slopes multiply to [MATH: -1,] we conclude that the line [MATH: y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x -5] is perpendicular to the given line.

So, the correct answer is "III only".

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Two lines are perpendicular if they intersect at a right angle. For example, the lines [MATH: {\color{red}y = 2x - 1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+5}] shown below are perpendicular:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/81aa2de5645d05769b37848e83376801]

Content:
We can tell whether two lines are perpendicular by looking at their slopes. In general,

Content:
> If two lines are perpendicular, then the product of their slopes is equal to [MATH: -1.]

Content:
We see this with the two lines graphed above: the lines [MATH: {\color{red}y = 2x - 1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+5}] have slopes [MATH: \color{red}2] and [MATH: {\color{blue}-\dfrac{1}{2}},] respectively. If we take the product of the slopes, we get

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}{\left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) }} = -1.]

Content:
Watch out! The only exception is for horizontal and vertical lines. Horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular, but the slope of a vertical line is undefined, so we cannot multiply it by anything.

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining Whether Two Lines in Slope-Intercept Form are Perpendicular

Example Prompt:
Which of the following lines is perpendicular to [MATH: y= -\dfrac{2}{5}x-3?]

1. [MATH: y = 5x + 1]
2. [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3]
3. [MATH: y = -\dfrac{x}{2} + 5]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For the two lines to be perpendicular, their slopes must multiply to [MATH: -1.]

The line [MATH: y=-\dfrac{2}{5}x-3] is in slope-intercept form, and its slope is [MATH: -\dfrac{2}{5}.]

Looking at the answer choices, the line [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3] has a slope of [MATH: \dfrac{5}{2}.]

Multiplying the slopes together, we have

[MATH: \left( -\dfrac{2}{5}\right) \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} = -1.]

Since the slopes multiply to [MATH: -1,] we conclude that the line [MATH: y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3] is perpendicular to the given line.

So, the correct answer is "II only".
